title: Al-Azhar in Cairo
hook: the mosque and university founded by the Fatimids, later a great center of Sunni learning

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cairo founded: the Fatimids built a new city beside the Nile and called it al-Qahira. Your line was: the victorious city. Did you find it on a map? Day nine hundred forty-seven.

A student sits on a mat with his back against a stone column. A teacher sits against the next column over, and a small ring of students has gathered around him. Another ring sits by the next pillar, and another by the one after that. Nobody has a desk. Some have a book on their knees, some have only their memory. That is what a class looks like in this mosque: a circle on the floor, gathered beside a pillar. The new city beside the Nile needed a great mosque, and its builders raised one close to the palaces. Today: al-Azhar in Cairo.
screen: `A RING OF STUDENTS BY A PILLAR.` → `NO DESKS, JUST A MAT.` → `A GREAT MOSQUE FOR A NEW CITY.`

segments.voice: Al-Azhar was built by the Fatimids, the Isma'ili dynasty from yesterday. Tradition explains the name as the radiant, or the shining one, and some connect it with Fatimah al-Zahra, the daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, from whom the Fatimids traced their line. Scholars give that link with a little caution, and so should we. At first it taught the Isma'ili teaching of its founders. Later, when the Fatimid age ended and new rulers held Egypt, the mosque came to teach Sunni learning, and in time it became one of the places Sunni students traveled toward: the Qur'an, hadith, law, Arabic grammar, the sciences that serve the text. So one building carried two chapters of Islamic history. That's worth saying plainly, without ranking either one. Why travel so far to sit on a mat by a pillar? The Qur'an has a short prayer for that kind of hunger, one it teaches the Prophet to say. In Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Not increase me in wealth, or in fame. Knowledge. In those rings, learning was done in a mosque, between the prayers, close to worship. A class could stop for the call to prayer and pick up again after. And the method was the circle. A teacher read, explained, and answered. Students copied, memorized, questioned, and when a teacher judged a student ready, gave permission to teach in turn. People today speak of al-Azhar as a thousand years of study. Whatever the exact count, the picture is the same: someone, by a pillar, reading.
screen: `THE FATIMIDS BUILD A MOSQUE.` · `ONE BUILDING, TWO CHAPTERS.` · `MY LORD! INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.` · `A TEACHER, A PILLAR, A CIRCLE.` · then, large: `A THOUSAND YEARS OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: The practice: study, the way those circles did. For the next two minutes, sit as if you've just joined a ring on the floor. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you've been meaning to understand better: a verse, a word, a question about this path, or anything at all you care about. Hold the question, not the answer. What exactly don't you know? If you pray, you can say the line the Qur'an teaches: My Lord! Increase me in knowledge. If you don't, let the question sit quietly. Later today, give it fifteen minutes of real study. The bell holds the time.
Al-Azhar in Cairo. The mosque the Fatimids built in their new city, which later became a place of Sunni learning, taught in circles by the pillars. Today's word.
Your line: a thousand years of study. Today, give fifteen minutes to learning one thing properly, with a book, a notebook, or a good question. Day nine hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Al-Azhar is still a working mosque and a place of Islamic learning in Cairo, and students study the Qur'an, hadith, law and Arabic there, some in circles around a teacher.

"My Lord! Increase me in knowledge" (20:114, Pickthall).

fork.setup: you're a student who has traveled far to Cairo. there are many teachers in the mosque, each by a different pillar. what do you do?
options: wait for a classroom with desks to open.
join a ring on the floor by a pillar.
study alone from books you brought.
fork.reveal: you sit down in a circle. the teacher reads and explains, students copy, memorize and ask, and the class pauses for prayer.

what it means: a mosque where classes met in circles by the pillars, and learning sat between the prayers.
what a scholar hears: an Isma'ili foundation that later became a Sunni center, and a name some link, with caution, to Fatimah al-Zahra.
